source.title: Discovering Divergent Representations Between Text-To-Image Models
source.authors: Lisa Dunlap; Joseph Gonzalez; Trevor Darrell; Fabian Caba Heilbron; Josef Sivic; Bryan C. Russell

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the convergence hypothesis and says CompCon could be used to probe it, but its results compare generated image attributes rather than representational distances or alignment as models scale.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative, prompt-conditioned output differences between text-to-image models. These bear on model-specific semantic behavior but do not measure the claim's representational alignment. The ID2 benchmark scores compare discovery methods, not convergence, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds a method (CompCon) to discover prompt-conditioned output differences between text-to-image models and benchmarks it on ID2. It never measures representational alignment, mappings, shared features, or how similarity changes with scale. It only mentions the Platonic hypothesis as something the tool could probe. Its findings are output-level differences, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude CompCon systematically reveals subtle, input-dependent differences between text-to-image models, including stylistic and social biases. They suggest it could probe the Platonic convergence hypothesis, but they do not test it.
record.recipe_differences: The study discovers qualitative output-level differences; it does not apply the original studies' representational-alignment methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that the initial prompt set affects discovered descriptions and that VLM/LLM choice and iteration count affect discovery results.

fits_no_version.finding: CompCon finds prompt-conditioned visual associations that differ between text-to-image models, such as wet streets, decay, flames, and demographic biases. Some of these divergences recur across model pairs: PixArt with Playground, and SD-Lightning with Dreamlike. The authors speculate this reflects aesthetic-curated training data rather than a shared base model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-to-image models differ in output-level semantic–visual associations, and these differences group by training data rather than by architecture backbone.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) 2025
record.problems: The results relevant to model differences are qualitative and output-level. The paper does not measure representational distances or convergence, and its proposed explanation involving training data is speculative rather than causally tested.
record.rows_left_out: ID2 benchmark method-comparison scores and qualitative examples unrelated to cross-model output differences are omitted because they do not measure the claim.

untested.parts: No measure of alignment across model scale or capability.
No vision–language alignment on paired data.
No comparison across seeds of internal features.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
No neuron, SAE-feature or circuit comparison across models.
No representational similarity metric is varied.
No quantified alignment level or plateau. The training-data explanation is speculative only.

record.verdict_notes: The ID2 benchmark scores compare discovery methods and were rightly left out. The text's use of 'representation' means semantic-to-visual output associations, not internal embeddings.

versions.untested_parts: Alignment between independently trained models as size and capability increase; no scale or capability sweep.
No alignment measurement between vision and language models on paired images and captions, or comparison with model performance.
No comparison across random initializations or measurement of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No test for recurring interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.
No test of how representational convergence varies with similarity metrics, their settings, or input distributions.
The paper reports output-level differences and speculates about training data, but does not measure representational alignment, a plateau, or the causal role of shared data or objectives.

rows.subject: PixArt and SD-Lightning
rows.operation_detail: Compared generated images for prompt-conditioned visual attributes

conditions.value: negative emotions or empty urban environments

rows.measure: Qualitative presence of wet streets in generated images
rows.value: The paper reports that PixArt associates these prompts with wet streets.
rows.note: The reported difference is in generated image content, not a representational-distance or convergence measure.
rows.check: Qualitative output-level difference found by the study's own discovery method. It is not a representational alignment measure, so its state cannot bear on any version.

rows.subject: PixArt and SD-Lightning
rows.operation_detail: Compared generated images for prompt-conditioned visual attributes

conditions.value: well-kept or new elements placed in abandoned or neglected settings

rows.measure: Qualitative depiction of decay or dilapidation
rows.value: The paper reports that PixArt associates abandonment with decay, while SD-Lightning struggles to depict rundown or dilapidated scenes.
rows.note: An output-level difference; the study does not quantify representational alignment.
rows.check: Qualitative output difference, partly a prompt-adherence failure in SD-Lightning. No convergence measure.

rows.subject: PixArt and SDXL-Lightning
rows.operation_detail: Compared generated images for prompt-conditioned visual attributes

conditions.value: strong emotions, including anger, grief, and resilience

rows.value: The paper reports flames in PixArt outputs but not SDXL-Lightning outputs for the discovered prompts.
rows.note: This is a qualitative output divergence, not a measurement of geometric similarity.
rows.check: Qualitative output difference (flames); the figure is an illustration of the method's output. No convergence measure.

rows.subject: PixArt and Playground 2.5
rows.operation_detail: Compared discovered output differences across model pairs
rows.measure: Qualitative presence of fire or flames
rows.value: The paper reports that strong emotions are associated with fire in both PixArt and Playground when compared with other models.
rows.note: The authors speculate that similarities between PixArt and Playground may reflect their focus on curating highly aesthetic images; this is not tested causally.
rows.check: Shared divergence between PixArt and Playground is qualitative. The attribution to training data is the authors' speculation and untested, so it cannot bear on V7.

rows.subject: SD-Lightning and Dreamlike
rows.operation_detail: Compared discovered output differences across model pairs
rows.measure: Qualitative depiction of women with glasses and short hair
rows.value: The paper reports this association for SD-Lightning and Dreamlike.
rows.note: The paper presents this as a shared output difference, not as evidence of representational convergence.
rows.check: Qualitative shared bias in outputs. It is not a representational similarity measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
